taels from Bombay to Shanghai, he brought along his first
lieutenant, **J. M. Lavey**, who had been head of ... Sassoon &
Co. in Calcutta. Hardheaded, energetic, reserved, Commander
Lavey is the picture of an English squire. His career began
at sea when he was sixteen. He later qualified as a master
mariner which he likes to be addressed. During an interlude
in his seafaring he became a journalist, managing a group of
British newspapers for several years. He met Sir Victor
in the war, and thereafter was persuaded to take up the study
of private banking. At this he is now past master. His
realistic hand is also laid upon the various Sassoon land
companies, together with the Yangtze Finance Co. and the Inter-
national Investment Trust.

Between the Commander and Sir Victor there is a profound
friendship, based not upon likes but upon opposites. Both live
in the Cathay Hotel, both are bachelors. The quality of
bachelordom, however, is not a constant, and the Commander's
is as different from Sir Victor's as day is from night. No
doubt he watches over the pranks of his imaginative associate
with a somewhat fatherly eye. He seldom goes to clubs, plays
no golf, and at the most convivial party (usually one of Sir
Victor's) prefers to buttonhole a willing guest and discuss
the silver situation in the corner.

The U.S. has at last reached a dominant position in
... i trade, but the American Shanghaiander owes few thanks
to Congress or to the foreign policy of the White House. Once
upon a time, after America had first secured the advantage
of extraterritoriality in 1844, the clipper ships crossed the
Pacific rapidly and American shipping won first place in
that international port. But the clippers became obsolete.
American shipping all but vanished from the China Sea. The
American foreign policy, never distinguished for its firmness
in any direction, set no new forces to work. While successive
Secretaries of State continued to hold apologetically to the
principle of extraterritoriality, American business was forced
to seek, with no little shame, the protection of British guns.
American traders left Shanghai, and left behind them no American
bank, and only memories of those two great American trading and
shipping houses, Russell & Co. and Olyphant & Co.

However, the U.S. never quite lost her place in China.
The thousands of U.S. missionaries did not go out to trade, but
they did carry on a spiritual warfare that had material reper-
cussions in America as well as in China. Religious, philan-
thropic, and educational societies invested from $40,000,000
to $50,000,000 (gold), which is equal to the investment of all
other nations put together; and the annual U.S. remittances
to Chinese missions, etc. traditionally in the millions of
dollars and totaling $8,000,000 (gold) in 1928, have always
played a certain part in balancing China's international trade.
Much of this money went to the endowment and support of schools,
two dozen colleges, and half a dozen big universities, where
ambitious Chinese students become acquainted with the wonders
of the big democracy across the Pacific. In missions and
especially in missionary higher education, America has been
consistently to the fore. The butt of sneer and jest from the
businessman, the missionary has usually been "on the side of
the natives" and has rarely asked for gun protection.

The American commercial advance in China was resumed
toward the end of the 19th century when the Standard Oil Co.
outgrew its American market for kerosene. Learning that
400,000,000 Chinese were burning sesame oil in their lamps,
Mr. Rockefeller set forth to tap that enormous market in the
nineties. With its headquarters in Shanghai, his company
expanded until its house name, Mei Foo, became a passport to
the most distant villages of the interior. Other American

the wake of Standard Oil, the Sun Maid Raisin Growers Association
distributed its surplus far and wide by suggesting to the
Chinese mother that raisins would bless her with a boy. Anderson
Meyer & Co. experimented successfully with a general export and
import business; and the U.S. flag appeared more frequently in
Shanghai waters when the Pacific Mail established a semimonthly
service. And in 1904 Frank Jay Aven, the first of the modern
American bankers, came to Shanghai to set up a group of banks
and loan companies.

Thereafter the pace accelerated. The National City is
now the biggest financial agent in the Yangtze, making no
important investments, but financing millions of dollars'
worth of trade. In 1919 R. Aven was joined by Cornelius
Vander Starr, who proceeded to make Shanghai the insurance
centre of the Orient. After the World War one began to hear that
Henry Ford was about to revolutionize China with hundreds of
millions to be spent in building roads, but nothing ever
came of this, and Ford has no plant in China. Meanwhile,
and during the roaring twenties, there came a flock of U.S.
companies whose stocks were soaring in New York—General Motors
Corp., E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., Eastman Kodak Co., the
National Mining, Chemical Co., and Colgate-Palmolive-Peet.
American grocers, led by Wang, Culbertson & Fritz, installed
bat cricks or telephones on the land, which put into the discard
the old exchange operator who called on his customers with
pony and trap. In 1925 the China Trade Act was passed by
Congress; by 1925 U.S. firms were given roughly the same tax
privileges as the British had enjoyed all along; and in 1926
an income-tax ruling protected the incomes of the taipans from
the clutches of Washington. In 1929 Sidney Mitchell's Electric Bond & Share bought Shanghai's
municipal power plant for $32,000,000 (gold) and proceeded under
Taipan Hopkins to make the Shanghai Power Co. the biggest in the
Far East; while the Kahn Brothers' I.T. & T. bought the Shang-
hai Telephone Co., most polyglot in the world, for $4,000,000
(gold).

All this has swelled the American volume of business with
China, concentrated at Shanghai, with the result that the U.S.
now surpasses all competitors in volume of trade. But in one
branch of industry there are scarcely any competitors; the
U.S. has a virtual monopoly among foreigners in the air. This
came about in 1928 when Washington got rumors that the entire
civil aviation program of the Nanking Government was about to
be turned over to the German Luft Hansa. The State Department
got in touch with Aviation Exploration, Inc., a small syndicate
headed by Clement Melville Keys for the purpose of surveying new
air routes and turning the information to some line for
development. In March 1929, a group headed by William B.
Robertson, one of Lindbergh's backers, arrived in Shanghai with
a Curtiss Falcon mail plane, a Curtiss Robin training ship,
a Loening, and a small flying boat. After various vicissitudes,
the China National Aviation Corp. was set up and now has a non-
monopoly contract with the Chinese Government, good until 1940.
45 per cent of its stock, originally controlled by Interconti-
nental Aviation Inc., was eventually bought by young Juan Terry
Trippe's Pan American, and the real development was on passenger
lines carrying mail on a per-pound basis now link Shanghai with

American planes with American pilots backed by American capital.
Chinese are trained as second pilots, whereupon many of them
join the Chinese Army. The Chinese are reputedly better aviators
than the Japanese and are building a big air fleet. Through the
contracts gained by establishing air routes, American aviation

此后，步伐加快。花旗银行（National City Bank）现在是长江流域最大的金融代理机构，虽不进行重大投资，但为数百万美元的贸易提供融资。1919年，R. 阿文迎来了科尼利厄斯·范德·斯塔（Cornelius Vander Starr），后者着手将上海打造为东方的保险中心。第一次世界大战后，人们开始听说亨利·福特打算投入数亿美元修建道路，从而彻底改变中国，但这事最终不了了之，福特在中国没有设立工厂。与此同时，在喧嚣的二十年代，一大批在美国纽约股价飙升的美国公司涌入——通用汽车公司、E. Robertson）率领的一个团队抵达上海，带有一架柯蒂斯猎鹰式邮政飞机、一架柯蒂斯罗宾式教练机、一架洛宁式飞机和一艘小型水上飞机。经历各种波折后，中国航空公司（China National Aviation Corp.）成立，目前与中国政府签有一份非垄断合同，有效期至1940年。其45%的股份最初由洲际航空公司（Intercontinental Aviation Inc.）控制，最终被年轻的胡安·特里普（Juan Terry Trippe）的泛美航空公司买下，真正的发展在于客运航线，这些航线按每磅邮件的基础携带邮件，如今将上海与北平、南京、广州、汉口、重庆、成都以及沿途站点连接起来。沿长江的重要内陆航线由美国飞机飞行，由美国资本支持的美国飞行员驾驶。中国人被训练为副驾驶，随后许多人加入中国军队。据称中国人的飞行技术优于日本人，并且正在建立一支庞大的空军舰队。通过建立航线所获得的合同，美国航空业

Shelter: A bachelor will probably live in one of
Sir Victor Sassoon's smart new apartments, but a married
man more likely in a house in the western roads area or
in the outskirts of Frenchtown with two or three extra

rates run from 12 to 16 per cent of real or assessed
rental. In the western roads area, one has to Chinese
sovereignty by paying a flat land tax of $5 a year.
No taxes, business or personal.

Servants: From 10 to 20. The minimum includes a
No. 1 boy (a kind of butler) at $50 per month, plus a
recognized squeeze of 5 per cent on supplies, plus
Chinese (tip), plus on the Chinese New Year (usually
February); Number Two boy at $25; Number One cook at $35,
Number Two at $15; two house coolies at $18; an amah for
his tai-tai (wife) at $25; wash and sewing amah at $20;
Chinese chauffeur at $60; governess at from $50 (Russian)
to $200 (English). All the servants except the governess
take their squeeze on such purchases as they can, but it
rarely exceeds 5 per cent and the net costs of the goods is
far below what the taipan himself would have to pay. Total
servants about $7,000 a year.

In addition, possibly, ponies and grooms to look after
them at $20. The ponies cost $250 or more each. House-
boat would come higher - $1,000 (Chinese) to $50,000 (foreign).
The boat's laodah (captain, or literally, Big Old Man) gets
$20, but is the biggest squeeze taker on the staff. The
engineer under him gets $25 because he understands machinery.
Two coolies at $10. This is an average crew.

Special Note: If you treat a Chinese servant with
understanding he will take sharp reductions in pay when you
are down in your luck; will even, in extreme cases, feed
you out of his savings. In good times he expects the reverse
treatment.

Food: Imported goods such as shredded beef and
Campbell's soup come much higher than in the U.S., native
products much lower. The best dairies are American or
English operated. There are also American vegetable farms
whose products, unlike the native gardeners', are not
fertilized with human excrement.

Clothing: Men buy shirts, pajamas, and underwear on
Fifth Avenue, Manhattan, or Bond Street, London, and then
have them copied by native shirtmakers in Shanghai for years
thereafter. Shoes are the most difficult item; most taipans
and their wives bring back dozens on their return from home
leave. Men find that native dressmaking is erratic and
dowdy, best at underwear and accessories, which can be
copied from foreign models. But there is hope in the Russian
modistes.

住房：单身汉可能住在维克多·沙逊爵士（Sir Victor Sassoon）时尚的新公寓里，但已婚男子更可能住在西区道路区域或法租界边缘的房屋中，带有两三个额外房间；如果是租赁，后者每月费用为750美元；如果是自有，则代表15,000美元的投资。土地税低于评估价值的1%；捐税率为实际租金或评估租金的12%至16%。在西区道路区域，通过每年缴纳5美元的固定土地税，人们处于中国主权之下。无商业或个人所得税。

仆人：10至20人。最低配置包括一名一号男仆（一种管家），月薪50美元，外加公认的采购回扣5%，外加小费，外加中国新年（通常在二月）红包；二号男仆25美元；一号厨师35美元，二号厨师15美元；两名家务苦力各18美元；为其太太（妻子）服务的阿妈25美元；洗衣缝纫阿妈20美元；中国司机60美元；家庭女教师从50美元（俄罗斯人）到200美元（英国人）不等。除家庭女教师外，所有仆人都能在他们经手的采购中获取回扣，但很少超过5%，且商品的净成本远低于大班本人必须支付的价格。仆人总费用每年约7,000美元。

此外，可能还有马匹和马夫照料它们，费用20美元。每匹马花费250美元或更多。 houseboat（中式游艇/画舫）费用更高——1,000美元（中式）至50,000美元（西式）。船老大（船长，字面意思为“大老”）薪水20美元，但是职员中拿回扣最多的人。他手下的工程师薪水25美元，因为他懂机械。两名苦力各10美元。这是一个平均配置的船员班子。

特别说明：如果你以理解的态度对待中国仆人，当你运气不好时，他会大幅降低工资要求；在极端情况下，甚至会用他的积蓄供养你。在好时光里，他期望得到相反的待遇。

食物：进口商品如碎牛肉和坎贝尔汤比在美国贵得多，本土产品则便宜得多。最好的奶场由美国人或英国人经营。还有美国蔬菜农场，其产品不像本地菜农那样使用人粪施肥。

服装：男士在曼哈顿第五大道或伦敦邦德街购买衬衫、睡衣和内衣，然后在此后多年里让上海的本地裁缝复制。鞋子是最难办的项目；大多数大班及其妻子在回国休假归来时会带回几十双。男士发现本地裁缝制作水平不稳定且俗气，最擅长制作内衣和配饰，这些可以仿制外国款式。但俄罗斯女时装设计师带来了一线希望。

汽车：主要是一种社交必需品，尽管良好的道路现在开始深入中国乡村，为上海居民提供了他通常从未见过的东西：中国。最受欢迎的汽车是福特，

**Schools:** prior to the age of twelve the British
children are in the hands of a governess or at
Shanghai's excellent private cathedral school; after that
they go on for finishing. The American citizen sends
his children to the American school (Colonial brick) until
they are ready for college. Most nationalities support
their own schools, but parental instinct is not the
only part of Shanghai's neurasthenic stress; there is no
public system possible.

**Entertainment:** expensive because so constant and so
varied. Biggest item: liquor. For private parties, homes
are supplemented by hotels and the more respectable cabarets.
Figure $5,000, plus another $5,000 for bills contracted at
half a dozen clubs.

**Charity:** a small item. The French support many of
their charities on a 40 per cent cut ($2,000,000 a year)
from the revenues of the dog track and jai alai operators
in Frenchtown. The Americans have a Community Chest that
is large enough to look after indigent Yankees and also contributes
to the Fourth of July and Washington's Birthday balls.
The Shanghailander's next act (though he rarely talks about
it) is to provide, with feudal self-satisfaction, for his
expatriates or the unfortunate relatives of his staff.
Maybe $1,000.

**Religion:** an even smaller item. British taipan's
firm buys him a pew in the Holy Trinity Cathedral. He goes
on state occasions. American taipans have no pew bought for
them. Consistent nonattendance at the American Community
Church costs them $100 a year.

**Hospitals:** because of the amount and variety of disease,
they are large, well-run, inexpensive. The two best are the
Shanghai General Hospital on Soochow Creek, staffed by the
Franciscan Missionaries of Mary; the Country Hospital on
Great Western Road, where the nurses are prettier, the surroundings
more cheerful. Both are operated by the Municipal
Council. Not to be overlooked is the new Battle Creek Sanitarium,
dispensing the health foods and regime of Battle
Creek, Michigan.

**Gambling:** at the end of a year of reasonable expenditures
should equal some $15,000. This is for the New York
Stock Exchange, a weekly poker game, a small chunk of Shanghai
real estate.

**〔此处转录不清〕**

**学校：** 十二岁之前，英国儿童由家庭女教师照顾，或就读于上海优秀的私立教会学校；之后他们继续接受 finishing school（精修学校/女子精修学校）教育。美国公民将子女送入美国学校（殖民风格砖建筑），直到他们准备上大学。大多数国籍的人都支持自己的学校，但父母的本能并非上海神经衰弱压力的唯一部分；这里不可能存在公共教育体系。

**娱乐：** 昂贵，因为既频繁又多样。最大项目：酒类。私人聚会之外，还有酒店和较正派的歌舞厅作为补充。估算5,000美元，另外5,000美元用于在六七个俱乐部产生的账单。

**慈善：** 小额项目。法国人依靠法租界赛狗场和回力球运营商收入的40%抽成（每年200万美元）来支持他们的许多慈善机构。美国人有一个社区基金（Community Chest），规模足以照顾贫困的美国同胞，并资助独立日和华盛顿诞辰舞会。上海居民的下一步行动（虽然他很少谈论此事）是以封建式的自我满足感，供养他的侨民同胞或其职员的不幸亲属。也许1,000美元。

**宗教：** 更小的项目。英国大班的商行为他在圣三一堂购买了一个座位。他在正式场合前往。美国大班没有为他们购买座位。坚持不参加美国社区教堂使他们每年花费100美元。

**医院：** 由于疾病种类繁多且数量大，医院规模大、管理良好、费用低廉。最好的两家是位于苏州河畔、由玛利亚方济各传教修女会 staffed 的上海广慈医院（Shanghai General Hospital）；以及位于大西路（Great Western Road）的乡村医院（Country Hospital），那里的护士更漂亮，环境更令人愉快。两者均由工部局运营。不可忽视的是新的巴特尔克里克疗养院（Battle Creek Sanitarium），它提供密歇根州巴特尔克里克的健康食品和养生法。

**赌博：** 在一年合理支出的末尾，应相当于约15,000美元。这包括纽约证券交易所的交易、每周一次的扑克游戏、一小块上海房地产。
